title: Unemployment Insurance Reform
summary: Reform unemployment insurance (UI) to stabilize workers' economic security and the economy by expanding eligibility to include gig and contract workers, low-wage workers, and workers displaced by AI; increasing benefit amounts and duration to a minimum floor of 30 weeks, including by indexing benefit levels to regional costs of living; and modernizing the tax contribution base so that program financing matches effective benefits delivery.
rationale:
The cash support that UI benefits provide gives workers an essential lifeline and buffer against the immediate effects of job loss. Job loss can easily have cascading effects on one's ability to maintain safe, secure housing, stable health care, and daily subsistence. AI could exacerbate this trend by eliminating 10 to 15% of U.S. jobs {{cite:bcg-reshape-jobs-2026}}, as estimated by Boston Consulting Group.

But even before AI's mainstream adoption, UI programs haven't kept up with the realities of today's labor market:

- In 2026, only about one in four eligible workers receive UI benefits {{citep:dol-ui-recipiency-2026}}. Younger, less educated, and racial and ethnic minority populations are less likely {{citep:wceg-ui-disparities-2022}} than older, more educated, non-minority populations to receive UI benefits because of misperceived ineligibility. Administrative burdens {{citep:nelp-unemployed-worker-2025}} like delayed decisions and difficulty navigating UI websites and UI agencies by phone also impose significant barriers on applicants. UI programs also exclude independent contractors and gig workers {{citep:fedcommunities-ui-takeup-2026}}.

- Long-term unemployment is rising, and current UI benefits are not enough. As of July 2026, there are 1.8 million long-term unemployed workers {{citep:bls-employment-situation-2026-07}} in the U.S., 45% and 55% more {{citep:cnbc-longterm-unemployment-2026}} than in 2019 and 2023 respectively.

- The wage base for the federal tax that employers pay to fund federal UI programs has failed to keep up with wage growth and inflation. UI taxable wage base has remained frozen at $7,000 since 1983; if adjusted for inflation, the Niskanen Center reports that this number should be $23,188 in November 2025 {{cite:niskanen-broaden-base-2025}}.
feasibility: Federal reform requires Congress to act. States administer benefits and would align to a new federal floor. The Pandemic Unemployment Assistance program in 2020 showed that coverage extensions can be deployed within weeks when political will exists. Most state systems run legacy computing infrastructure, so even fully funded reform takes years to roll out.
strengths: No regrets policy. The extent to which AI displaces workers remains to be seen, but policymakers should act now to ensure that our economic infrastructure supports workers when crises arise. As it stands, our outdated UI system is ill-equipped to address the problems like sudden surges in lay-offs, as demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic. The response led to immediate, temporary CARES Act measures like providing workers with an additional $600 weekly supplement and including excluded workers like self-employed and temporary workers. We can act now to mobilize faster crisis response and set workers up for success in the event of job loss by modernizing the UI system.

A modernized UI system is more robust and effective in stabilizing not just workers but the economy as a whole: job loss has ripple effects as families and households shrink consumer spending and stop buying non-essential goods and services, potentially leading to declining retail sales that can trigger more business contractions and lay-offs. A strong UI system provides a buffer for families and the economy.

To prepare for the scale of AI's impact on employment, UI programs can integrate automatic triggers based on different levels of AI-related mass unemployment. This approach can ensure that extended UI benefits kick in fast enough to catch families when they need support.
risks: States wield broad authority over determining UI eligibility and benefit levels. In fact, up until 2011, all 50 states offered up to 26 weeks {{citep:nelp-federal-ui-2024}} of UI benefits. Today, 16 states {{citep:cbpp-ui-weeks-2024}} provide fewer than 26 weeks of benefits. A federal standard can help set a floor for benefits, but differences in how each state ultimately determines eligibility mean that workers' protections will vary across states.

Raising the tax base that funds UI programs increases labor costs for businesses, which might be met with strong opposition from employers. In response, employers may hire fewer workers and cut workers' hours, abstain from giving workers raises or bonuses, or increase prices for goods and services to offset higher tax burdens.
landscape:
The Unemployment Insurance Modernization and Recession Readiness Act (S.2312 / H.R.4439), led by Senator Wyden, is the leading federal vehicle for comprehensive UI reform {{cite:wyden-ui-overhaul-2025}}.

Modernization has consistent bipartisan support in principle. The political fault line runs through coverage scope for gig workers and the financing base {{cite:epi-ui-financing-2021}}. New Jersey's S.1840 (2026) {{cite:148}} reflects growing state-level willingness to use the unemployment system as the displacement-response vehicle. State-level momentum is strongest in New Jersey, Washington, and Massachusetts.

Canada's Employment Insurance covers a broader range of work arrangements. Pandemic Unemployment Assistance (2020) demonstrated that coverage can be extended rapidly when political will exists. Several U.S. states have enacted independent expansions.

Washington State's expanded unemployment insurance coverage for gig workers offers a partial model; Massachusetts and New Jersey have enacted coverage extensions. The Pandemic Unemployment Assistance program showed that universal coverage is administratively achievable within weeks. The barriers are political, not logistical.

pairsWith.why: Both cushion lost earnings in a transition; wage insurance extends unemployment insurance from an income backstop to a re-employment top-up.
A functional unemployment-insurance baseline is a precondition for portable benefits, which lean on the same administrative plumbing.
